voice_script:
[curious] An AI system can now take a research question, choose an experiment, run the code on a lab's own computer, inspect the result, and suggest what to try next. Put that on screen and it looks less like a chatbot and more like a junior lab partner who never gets tired of running simulations. [thoughtful]On November 17, 2026, the company used its SC26 presentation to show this workflow, alongside new scientific models, datasets, and computing systems. By the end, you'll know exactly how the loop works, why it could speed up chemistry, climate modeling and engineering, and where a human still has to stop the machine before trusting an answer.

[thoughtful] Start with the research goal, not a request for a paragraph. The agent has to turn that goal into actions: define a hypothesis, choose a simulation or database, run it, and compare the output with what the scientist expected. It can also decide what information is missing and plan another test.

That makes it different from an ordinary chatbot. [confidently]A chatbot mainly predicts a response to your prompt. An agent keeps a working plan, uses tools, reads their results, and then chooses the next move. Think of it like a lab notebook connected to the instruments: the model writes the next instruction, the computer carries it out, and the result comes back for inspection.

The systems described at SC26 can run code and simulations on infrastructure controlled by researchers. That lets the agent work beside existing scientific software, where the data and tools already live.

Underneath, this is a loop of planning, tool use, evaluation, and replanning. The CPUs handle tool calls, operations, and gathering results, while accelerators do the heavy simulation work. But the agent still needs a real scientific question to guide it, and that brings us to what it can actually discover.

[curious] Now see what that means in chemistry. A scientist might ask which molecular shapes could attach to a target protein. The agent can break that question into hypotheses, select a simulation, run candidates, and inspect the structures that come back. It isn't discovering by intuition; it's narrowing a search by running tests.

[surprised]In the SC26 material, the company says an agent at Argonne National Laboratory accepted a prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, selected simulations, and identified two new binding sites. The model proposed, the simulator checked, and the result changed the next proposal.

That needs more than general conversation text. Nemotron for Science combines Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, scientific evaluations, an open chemistry dataset, and post-training recipes for specialized agents. LitmusBench v0.2 contains nearly 50,000 chemistry questions covering molecular properties, drug-discovery data, solubility, and how the body processes molecules.

Here's the practical takeaway: judge an agent by whether it chooses valid tools and gets measurable results, not by how convincing its explanation sounds. But even a good result needs the next checks. That's where the hardware and the wider scientific pipeline become important.

[thoughtful] That brings us to the part people don't see: the computing underneath. Scientific agents are useful only if they can call serious tools quickly enough to explore many possibilities. GPU-accelerated simulation handles repeated numerical work, from molecular dynamics to climate and engineering models. The accelerator isn't the scientist; it's a very fast test bench.

The agent sits above that bench. It decides which run is worth paying for, sends the job, waits for the output, and compares it with the goal. If the result is weak, it can change the inputs instead of asking a person to rewrite every command.

SC26 also connects this to Vera for climate, molecular and engineering simulations, and Rubin HPC for testing materials, molecules and designs. The point isn't that one model knows all of science. It's that the model, simulator, GPU system, and researcher can be joined into one repeatable pipeline.

[confidently]Why does that matter? The expensive part of discovery is often trying possibilities that fail. Faster simulation doesn't guarantee a breakthrough, but it can make more attempts affordable. And that only helps if the loop knows when a result is trustworthy.

[skeptical] But now ask the question the demo cannot answer: how do we know the agent is right? A fluent plan can still choose a bad simulation, misunderstand an output, or carry an error into the next step. Science can't use confidence as proof.

The reported examples show why checks have to sit inside the loop. The company says a KTH Royal Institute of Technology agent repaired broken GROMACS molecular-dynamics setups, fixing 81% of test cases in one overnight run. Each fix was independently checked by GROMACS. That's much stronger than the agent simply claiming success.

[serious]The check has to come from the scientific software, a benchmark, a simulation, or a researcher with the right expertise. The company's guidance says verification can require computational or real-world data and may take hours or days. One wrong assumption can derail the task.

So if you use a system like this, give it a bounded job, not control of the whole lab. Define the goal, limit the tools, inspect the output, and run an independent check. Keep the inputs and logs so someone can reproduce what happened. That's how a fast assistant becomes useful evidence, rather than a confident guess.

[warmly] Simple version: the agent turns a research goal into a plan, uses scientific tools, checks results, and suggests the next test. GPUs speed simulations, but verification decides whether the answer is worth believing.
